text: Lesson 10 defined health factor as collateral value times liquidation threshold, divided by borrowed value, and noted it falls automatically as collateral's price drops. Liquidation is what happens the moment that number crosses below 1.0 — not a penalty applied after the fact, but a threshold that makes a position eligible for anyone to act on.

Take a position of 1 ETH collateral at 2,000 USDC, with 1,000 USDC borrowed and an 80% liquidation threshold. Health factor starts at 1.60 — safe. ETH drops to 1,200 USDC, and the health factor falls to 0.96. Nothing about the loan changed. A pure market price move was enough to cross the line.

A liquidator isn't the protocol team — it's any address, usually an automated bot, that calls the contract's public liquidate function once a position is eligible. In exchange for repaying part of the debt, it seizes a slightly larger dollar value of collateral. That difference is the liquidation bonus.

Say the liquidator repays 500 USDC of the debt, a common 50% cap, with a 5% bonus. They seize 525 USDC worth of ETH — at 1,200 per ETH, that's about 0.4375 ETH. Their profit is 25 USDC for repaying the debt. The borrower is left with 0.5625 ETH collateral against 500 USDC debt.

Any address can call liquidate the instant a position crosses the threshold — no queue, no case review, no employee deciding who goes first. Specialized bots monitor every position's health factor continuously and race each other, often paying extra gas, to capture the bonus first.

That competition is what keeps the system solvent — slow or discretionary liquidations would let undercollateralized debt pile up faster than anyone could clean it up. Next: flash loans, and how a loan with zero collateral is possible at all.
